chunks: I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about a man who slaughtered an animal but was ignorant that he should face it toward the qiblah. He said: 'Eat from it.'

So I said to him: 'What if he (intentionally) did not face it (toward the qiblah)?' He said: 'Then do not eat from it, and do not eat from any slaughtered animal upon which the Name of God, Mighty and Majestic, was not pronounced.'
And he (peace be upon him) said: 'When you intend to slaughter, face the qiblah with your animal.'

key_terms.اسْمُ اللَّهِ: The Name of God — the basmala (Bismillah) or tasmiya pronounced over the animal at the moment of slaughter; its omission renders the slaughter invalid
key_terms.الْقِبْلَة: Qiblah — the direction of the Ka'bah in Mecca, which Muslims face in prayer and, according to Shia fiqh, during ritual slaughter
key_terms.جَهِلَ: Was ignorant — a key jurisprudential distinction; ignorance (jahl) mitigates the ruling, unlike intentional omission
key_terms.ذَبِيحَة: Slaughtered animal; the act of ritual slaughter (dhabh) according to Islamic law

ai.seo_question: Is an animal permissible to eat if the slaughterer forgot to face the qiblah?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him) distinguishes between inadvertent and intentional failure to face the qiblah when slaughtering. An animal slaughtered by someone who was ignorant of the requirement is permissible to eat; however, if the person knowingly did not face the qiblah, the meat is forbidden. The Imam also states that neglecting to pronounce the name of God over the animal at slaughter renders its meat impermissible, and gives a direct command to face the qiblah when slaughtering.
